analysis.one_liner: Taxes big corporate owners $20,000 per home over 100, pushing them to sell houses to families.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or a Senate vote and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have charged large owners — hedge funds, private equity, and other corporate landlords — $20,000 per year for every single-family home they own beyond 100, with an annual requirement to sell off 10% of their holdings. Money raised would fund down payment assistance for families buying homes, with priority given to homes the big owners sell. It never got a hearing in the Senate Finance Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary families trying to buy their first home. The bill would push big corporate landlords to sell tens of thousands of houses into the market, and the tax revenue would fund down payment assistance grants through state housing finance agencies, with priority for families buying homes sold by those large owners.

how_it_helps.text: Large corporate landlords owning more than 100 single-family homes would owe $20,000 per home above 100 each year unless they sold at least 10% of their portfolio annually, pressuring them to sell houses to individual buyers.

Revenue from the tax would go into a Housing Trust Fund for HUD grants to state housing finance agencies for down payment assistance, with priority for families buying homes sold by these large owners.

analysis.who_pays: Large investors — hedge funds, private equity firms, and other entities owning more than 100 single-family homes — who would owe $20,000 per excess home per year and would bear the cost of selling down their portfolios. Some renters in homes sold off could face changes in landlords during the transition.

drawbacks.text: The 10% annual sell-off requirement is gradual: a giant owner starting from 100,000 homes would still hold a large portfolio for many years, so relief for buyers would build slowly.

The tax and reporting duties could add compliance costs and friction to housing transactions, and some economists argue large rental owners supply rental housing that some families need; forcing sales could tighten that market in some places.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — pressuring corporate owners to sell houses to families and funding down payments — is real and addresses a widely felt problem: high rents and unreachable home prices. The costs are modest for ordinary people: some analysts note that restricting bulk owners could reduce rental supply in some markets, and small landlords just over the threshold would face the tax. The main weakness is design: the tax escalator makes the initial phase slow, and the bill never advanced far enough to be refined or debated.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate, referred to the Finance Committee, and sat there without a hearing or vote until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023, killing the bill.

narrative.text: Sen. Merkley introduced the bill on November 30, 2022, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill's only actions after introduction were the reading and committee referral; the Finance Committee took no action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporate landlords and other big owners of single-family rental homes, who face no federal limit or tax on home hoarding, are better off because the bill died. Families hoping for help buying a home gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on November 30, 2022.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill took no action; no hearing, markup, or vote occurred before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors from either party, so no party-line vote ever occurred; it died without any record of position-taking by other senators.

industries.industry: Institutional single-family rental owners (large hedge funds, private equity, REITs)
industries.note: Owners above 100 single-family homes would face a $20,000-per-excess-home annual tax unless they sold 10% of their portfolio each year, pushing them to divest. The bill was designed to shrink their footprint in the for-sale housing market.

industries.industry: First-time homebuyers and families seeking down payment help
industries.note: Families would benefit from more homes coming onto the market and from trust fund grants for down payment assistance, prioritized for homes sold by large corporate owners.
Entities primarily engaged in building or rehabilitating single-family homes are explicitly excluded from the tax, so they could continue operating at scale.
